newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Concerns raised on W.Australia title changes.
newsitem.headline: Concerns raised on W.Australia title changes.

text.p: Holders of mining titles in Western Australia face considerable uncertainty under changes which make them responsible in future for any native title compensation, the state Chamber of Minerals and Energy said on Wednesday.
The Western Australia government said the measure which took effect on Tuesday was similar to approaches in other states.
Mines Minister Kevin Minson said it followed Native Title Tribunal decisions which said mining leases could be granted but that any compensation was to be dealt with at a future date.

"I know the industry is not happy with the situation we now find ourselves in, but as a responsible government we cannot disregard unknown liabilities of this type for future taxpayers," he said in a statement.
The state was responsible for any compensation from titles issued before Tuesday, he said.

Chamber executive officer Simon Williamson told Reuters the mining industry was comfortable with paying compensation when its activities impacted on people who held title over and had valid interests in land.
Western Australia, Australia's biggest mining state, produces 43 percent of the nation's mineral and energy output and ranks as a major international supplier of raw materials and processed metals.

Williamson said it currently was impossible to estimate what level of compensation the industry could face in Western Australia, as the federal Native Title Tribunal had not made any determination on compensation and the only claim granted to date gave no guide.
"We are concerned, however, that the liability that the native title compensation represents is unknown and introduces considerable uncertainty for any body contemplating a project," he told Reuters.

Williamson said the Chamber had been working with the government on the issue and was also discussing ways to minimise the industry's exposure and uncertainty by establishing principles to ensure compensation was determined upfront.
Native title claims had been lodged for about 72 percent of land in Western Australia, although none had yet been determined, officials said.
"Really we are dealing with a totally unknown liability... surely it is going to range over a spectrum (from) something quite minimal to something quite substantial," he said.
